analogy.p: Imagine a bag that holds numbered tickets from 1 to 6. Calling random(1,6) is like putting your hand in the bag and pulling out one ticket, reading the number, and then dropping it back in before the next person tries. The numbers on the tickets are the lower and upper limits: you can never pull out a 0 or a 7 because there is no such ticket. Taking the ticket home and writing the number on a card is like storing the result in a variable. Reaching in again is a new call and may give a different ticket. The analogy breaks down because a real bag really is unpredictable, whereas a computer's generator follows a calculation from a seed, so it is only pseudo-random; the same seed would give the same series of tickets.
analogy.t: A lucky dip bag with numbered tickets

bullets: A **random number** is a value chosen unpredictably from a range, e.g. a whole number from 1 to 6.
Random numbers are produced by a built-in **function** supplied by the language, so you do not have to write the maths yourself.
The range you give is made of a **lower limit** and an **upper limit**; the result is chosen between them.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language the call looks like **random(1,6)**; in Python it is **random.randint(1,6)** after importing the random library.
The result is normally stored in a **variable** so that it can be compared, displayed or used in a calculation.
Typical uses: dice and spinners in games, shuffling or picking items, choosing a random question, placing enemies or items at random, and simulating real-world chance.
Exam questions normally ask you to **write** a few lines using a random number, **complete** missing code, or **explain** what a given line does.
core.h: What random number generation is and why programs need it
core.p: **Random number generation** means asking the computer to produce a number that cannot be predicted in advance, usually within a range that you choose. In the J277 specification it sits in **2.2 Programming fundamentals** alongside the other basic tools of a programmer: variables, operators, selection, iteration and string handling. Without it, a program would behave identically every time it was run, which would make dice games, card shuffles, quizzes that pick a random question and many simulations impossible. You must be able to **use** random numbers in code you write and **read** code that uses them in the exam.

bullets: Syntax: **x = random(1,6)** stores a whole number from 1 to 6 in x.
**Inclusive** range: with random(1,6) every one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 is possible, and 0 and 7 are impossible.
The first argument is the **lowest** value and the second is the **highest** value; random(6,1) is back to front and bad practice.
The arguments can be **variables or expressions**, e.g. random(1, maxNumber) where maxNumber was input earlier.
The result is an **integer** (whole number), so it can be used directly as a list or array index or in a comparison with another integer.
Each separate call produces a **new** random value: random(1,6) written twice usually gives two different numbers.
To display the number you must **convert it to a string** if you join it to text, e.g. print("You rolled " + str(x)).
core.h: The OCR Exam Reference Language: random(low, high)
core.p: In OCR J277 papers, code is written in the **OCR Exam Reference Language** (ERL) or a high-level language of your choice such as Python. In ERL, random numbers are generated with a function that takes two arguments, the lowest and highest whole number allowed, written **random(low,high)**. The function **returns** a whole number, so you must assign it to a variable (or use it directly inside another statement) or the value is lost. Both limits are **inclusive**, meaning the answer can equal either limit.

bullets: **import random** must appear once, before any use of the library.
**random.randint(1,6)** returns an integer from 1 to 6, both ends included.
**random.randrange(1,6)** returns 1 to 5 only: the stop value is **excluded**, like range(). This is a common trap.
**random.random()** returns a decimal (float) from 0 up to but **not including** 1, which is useful for probability.
**random.choice(myList)** picks one item from a list at random, which avoids index calculations.
Calling the function with the wrong range gives wrong behaviour but usually **no error message**, so it is a **logic error**.
Leaving out import random gives a **NameError**, a run-time error because the name random is not defined.
core.p: Python does not have random numbers built in to the core language, so you must first **import the random library** at the top of the program using the line **import random**. After that you call functions from the library by writing random. in front of the function name. The most common function in GCSE work is **random.randint(a,b)**, which behaves like the OCR random(a,b): it returns a whole number from a to b **inclusive**. Forgetting the import line is a classic cause of an error that stops the program.

bullets: Dice with n sides: **random(1,n)**; a standard die is random(1,6).
Coin toss (two outcomes): **random(0,1)**, then let 0 mean heads and 1 mean tails (or the other way round) using an if statement.
Percentage: **random(1,100)** gives a whole number from 1 to 100.
Number from 50 to 100 inclusive: **random(50,100)**.
Random day of the week from a list of 7: random(0,6) when the list indexes start at 0.
Random age from 18 to 65 inclusive: **random(18,65)**.
If a question says a number 'between 1 and 10' and gives no more detail, a safe answer is random(1,10) and you may state the assumption.
core.h: Choosing the correct range: lower and upper limits
core.p: Most marks lost on this topic come from choosing the wrong range. You must work out the **smallest** and **largest** value the situation needs and use those as the two arguments. A standard six-sided die needs 1 to 6, so random(1,6). A coin can be modelled as 0 or 1, so random(0,1). A percentage chance needs 1 to 100. If you want a number between 10 and 20 inclusive, you write random(10,20), not random(10,19) or random(11,20). Always read the question for the words **inclusive**, **between** and **up to**.

bullets: **Pseudo-random** = looks random but is produced by an algorithm.
The **seed** is the starting value that the algorithm uses; a different seed (such as the current time) gives a different sequence.
The **same seed gives the same sequence**, which is useful for testing because a tester can reproduce a bug.
True randomness would need an unpredictable physical source (e.g. electrical noise), which ordinary GCSE code does not use.
Because the sequence is calculated, it is not suitable for high-security uses on its own; this is an extension point rather than a GCSE requirement.
Python's random library seeds itself automatically when the program starts, so you normally do not have to set it.
For an exam answer, say 'a random number is generated by the computer within the range given' unless the question asks how.
core.h: Pseudo-random numbers: how computers really make them
core.p: Computers are deterministic machines: they follow instructions exactly, so they cannot produce truly unpredictable numbers on their own. Instead they use an **algorithm** called a **pseudo-random number generator**. It begins with a starting value called a **seed** (often taken from the system clock) and performs a calculation to produce a sequence of numbers that **looks random** but is actually calculated. If you start with the same seed you get exactly the same sequence again. This is why the numbers are called **pseudo-random** rather than truly random. For GCSE purposes this is good enough for games and simulations.

bullets: Coin toss: **flip = random(0,1)** then **if flip == 0 then print("Heads") else print("Tails")**.
A **30% chance** event: n = random(1,100); **if n <= 30 then** the event happens (30 of the 100 values qualify).
A **1 in 6 chance** event, e.g. rolling a six: **if random(1,6) == 6**.
Use **elseif** or **elif** for several outcomes, e.g. 1 to 3 weak hit, 4 to 5 medium hit, 6 critical hit.
Use the **comparison operators** == , != , < , <= , > and >= to test the random value.
The value should be stored in a variable if you will use it more than once; calling random again inside each condition gives a **new** number each time.
The number of qualifying values divided by the total number of possible values gives the **chance** of the outcome.
core.h: Using random numbers with selection (if statements)
core.p: A random number on its own does nothing; it becomes useful when the program **makes a decision** using it. Selection compares the random value with a fixed number or range and runs different code depending on the result. This is how games decide whether you win, whether an enemy appears or which of several things happens. Thinking of it as a **probability** helps: if a random number from 1 to 10 is compared with 3, the chance of a number less than or equal to 3 is 3 in 10.

bullets: Pick a random item: **index = random(0, len(names) - 1)** then **print(names[index])**.
With 5 names the valid indexes are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so the range is random(0,4).
**len(names)** counts the items, so len(names) - 1 is always the highest index.
Using random(0, len(names)) is a classic **off-by-one error** because it can give an index that is one too big.
In Python, random.choice(names) does the same job safely in one step.
If the list is held with indexes starting at 1 (some pseudocode), adjust the range to random(1, n).
A random character from a string works the same way: word[random(0, len(word) - 1)].
Random numbers are also used to **shuffle** or to place data at random coordinates in a 2D array.
core.h: Using random numbers with lists, arrays and strings
core.p: Random numbers are often used as **indexes** to pick an item from a list or array. This is the method used in programs that choose a random question, name, card or colour. The key skill is getting the index range correct: lists start at **index 0** in most languages, so a list with n items has valid indexes **0 to n-1**. If you use a range that can reach n, the program will try to read an item that does not exist and crash with an index error. The same idea works for choosing a random character from a string.

bullets: Roll a die 10 times: **for i = 1 to 10** then **roll = random(1,6)** then **print(roll)** then **next i**.
Roll until a six: **do** roll = random(1,6) **until roll == 6**.
Generating the number **inside** the loop gives a new value each repeat; generating it **before** the loop gives the same value every repeat.
A **guessing game** picks the target number **once before** the loop, then loops asking for guesses, so the target stays the same while the player guesses.
A running **total** or **count** can be kept with a variable that is updated each time round, e.g. total = total + roll.
Using a **counter** such as attempts = attempts + 1 lets you report how many tries were needed.
Combine with a **while** loop plus a condition so the program stops at the right time.
core.p: Random numbers and loops are often combined. A loop may **repeat** an action using a fresh random value each time, such as rolling a die ten times, or may continue **until** a random event happens, such as a game that ends when you roll a six. A very common error is to generate the random number **outside** the loop and then expect it to change each time round the loop: it will not, because it was only generated once. If a new value is needed on every repeat, the call to random must be **inside** the loop.

bullets: **Single die:** roll = random(1,6) then print(roll).
**Two dice, total:** die1 = random(1,6); die2 = random(1,6); total = die1 + die2. Two separate calls are needed.
**Doubles:** if die1 == die2 then print("Double"). Compare the two stored variables.
**Guessing game:** target = random(1,20) once; loop: input guess; if guess < target say 'too low', if guess > target say 'too high', stop when equal.
**Random choice:** colours = ["red","blue","green"]; print(colours[random(0,2)]).
**Chance event:** if random(1,10) <= 2 then the item appears 20% of the time.
Trace carefully: a trace table for random code usually gives you the random values to use, because you cannot predict them yourself.
core.h: Worked patterns: dice, guessing games and chance events
core.p: A small set of patterns covers almost every exam question on this topic. Learn these as templates and then adapt the numbers. In each case, ask yourself three things: what is the **range**, **where** should the random number be generated (before or inside the loop), and **how** is the result going to be used (compare, display, index or calculate). Getting these three decisions right produces correct code first time.

bullets: **Possible outputs** of random(1,6): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 and nothing else.
The **boundary values** for random(1,6) are 1 and 6; a thorough tester checks the program works for both.
Replace random(1,6) with a **fixed number** (e.g. 6) temporarily to force a particular branch such as 'you win'.
A fixed seed gives a **repeatable** sequence so a tester can reproduce a fault.
In a trace table, copy down the random values given in the question into the column for that variable.
A **logic error** (e.g. wrong range) will not be reported by the computer; you only find it by checking the output against what was expected.
A **syntax error** (e.g. missing bracket) is caught before the program runs; a missing import causes a **run-time error**.
core.h: Testing and tracing code that uses random numbers
core.p: Random numbers make testing harder because the output is different every run. In the exam you will often be **given the random values** to trace through, or asked to say what the **possible outputs** are. When testing real programs, programmers check the **boundaries** of the range: the lowest and the highest values the generator can produce. They may also temporarily replace the random call with a **fixed value** so they can check that each branch of the program works, or fix the seed so the same sequence repeats. This links to the testing topic and to test data: normal, boundary and invalid.

bullets: **random(1,5)** when a six-sided die is needed: the 6 can never occur (range too small).
**random(0,6)** for a die: the 0 can occur, which is not a face of a die (range too big).
**random.randrange(1,6)** for a die: the 6 is excluded, so this only gives 1 to 5.
**random(0, len(list))** for an index: can give an index one past the end, causing an index error.
Calling random in the loop condition **and** again in the body so the two values differ and the logic breaks.
Not storing the value: a statement such as random(1,6) on its own line is lost because nothing receives the result.
Forgetting **import random** in Python, so the program stops with an error.
core.h: Common errors with random numbers: off-by-one and range mistakes
core.p: Examiners deliberately set code with a wrong range and ask you to spot the error, so recognise the usual faults. The most frequent is the **off-by-one error**, where the upper or lower limit is one too small or one too large. It happens because people forget whether the limits are inclusive. In OCR ERL and Python randint, they are inclusive. In Python's randrange and range, the stop value is excluded. A second family of errors is placing the call in the wrong place relative to a loop, and a third is forgetting to store the result.

bullets: **Selection:** random values are compared with if, elseif and else to choose between outcomes.
**Iteration:** random values can be created repeatedly in for or while loops, or used to end a loop.
**Data types and casting:** the result is an integer; use str() to join it to text and int() when converting input for comparison.
**Arrays and lists:** random indexes select items; the range must match the length of the structure.
**Subprograms:** a function such as rollDie() can return random(1,6) and be reused many times, helping with structured code.
**Testing:** boundary tests use the lowest and highest outputs; fixed values or seeds make results repeatable.
**Algorithms:** random choice appears in simple search or simulation, and in the 'guess the number' type of problem.
**Computational thinking:** abstraction lets a die be modelled as a random integer from 1 to 6.
core.p: Random numbers are rarely examined in isolation. They combine with the other programming fundamentals in J277 section 2.2 and appear in questions that ask you to write a short program, complete a flowchart or find an error. Understanding how they link helps you answer longer questions, especially the 8 to 12 mark programming questions where you must decide on variables, selection and loops yourself. They also link to algorithms, to testing and to data structures.

exam: **Command words:** 'Write' / 'Complete' means produce working code; 'State' means a short fact; 'Explain' needs a reason (because...); 'Identify the error' means point to the exact line and say what is wrong.
**1 mark:** give the **range** or a **possible value**, e.g. 'Give one number random(1,6) cannot produce' (answer 0 or 7).
**1 mark:** 'State what is meant by a random number' needs 'a number generated unpredictably within a range'.
**2 marks (code):** one mark for **storing** the result in a variable (x = ...), one mark for the **correct range** in random(low,high).
**3 to 4 marks (code):** two random calls with the correct range, the total or comparison, then a correct output statement, e.g. a two-dice program.
**Spotting errors:** check the **range** first, then whether the call is inside or outside the loop, then whether the result is stored, then the import (Python).
**Model phrases:** 'generates a random whole number between 1 and 6 inclusive', 'stored in the variable', 'a new random number is generated each time the loop repeats'.
**Pseudo-random:** if asked why a number is not truly random, say 'it is generated by an algorithm from a seed, so the same seed produces the same sequence'.
**Trace tables:** when random values are given, copy them in exactly; do not try to predict them. Update the variables line by line and watch loop conditions.
**6 mark programming question:** plan on paper: variables, range of random, loop type, selection, output. Comments and meaningful names help readability, and the code must actually work on the data.
**Testing questions:** boundary data for random(1,6) is 1 and 6; invalid data would be a number outside the range such as 0 or 7, which random(1,6) itself will never produce.
**Check:** read your range aloud: 'lowest possible, highest possible' and make sure both are really needed.

mistakes.r: With inclusive limits, random(1,6) can only give 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
mistakes.w: random(1,6) can give a 0 or a 7.

mistakes.r: Two dice need two separate calls, random(1,6) each, then add them; random(2,12) wrongly makes every total equally likely.
mistakes.w: The program rolls two dice with one call: die = random(2,12).

mistakes.r: A number generated once before the loop stays the same every repeat; generate it inside the loop for a new value each time.
mistakes.w: Calling random before a loop gives a new number each time round.

mistakes.r: The highest index is len(names) - 1, so the range must be random(0, len(names) - 1).
mistakes.w: Using random(0, len(names)) to choose from a list.

mistakes.r: randrange excludes the stop value, so it gives 1 to 5; use randint(1,6) for a die.
They produce pseudo-random numbers using an algorithm and a seed.
The returned value must be stored in a variable, e.g. roll = random(1,6), or used directly.
mistakes.w: Writing random(1,6) on a line by itself and expecting to use the answer.

mistakes.r: The library must be imported first, otherwise the program stops with an error.
Convert the number first: print("You rolled " + str(roll)).
mistakes.w: Joining a number to text directly: print("You rolled " + roll).

mistakes.r: The target must be chosen once before the loop, otherwise the player is chasing a moving number.
mistakes.w: The guessing game picks a new target inside the loop.

summary: The specification asks you to use random number generation within programs: producing a random whole number in a range with random(low,high) (or random.randint in Python), storing it, and using it with selection, iteration and lists. It matters because random values drive games and simulations and appear in short coding and error-spotting questions.

terms.d: A number produced unpredictably by the computer within a given range.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language, a function that returns a random whole number from low to high inclusive.
The Python function that returns a random integer from a to b, both limits inclusive.
Including the limit values themselves, e.g. 1 to 6 inclusive can give both 1 and 6.
Not including the limit, as in random.randrange(1,6) which never returns 6.
Produced by an algorithm so it appears random but is actually calculated from a starting value.
The starting value fed into a random number generator; the same seed gives the same sequence.
A collection of pre-written code, such as random, that can be imported and used in a program.
A statement that makes the code in a library available to the program, e.g. import random.
A named block of code that can return a value; random(1,6) is a function call that returns a value.
A value given to a function when it is called, such as the 1 and the 6 in random(1,6).
A named memory location that stores a value which can change while the program runs.
A data type for whole numbers with no decimal part.
The position of an item in a list or array, usually starting at 0.
A logic error where a limit or count is one too big or too small.
A mistake that lets the program run but produce the wrong result.
Test data at the very edge of the valid range, such as 1 and 6 for a die.
How likely an event is, found as favourable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes.

worked.q: Write a program in the OCR Exam Reference Language (or Python) that simulates rolling two six-sided dice, displays each die and the total, and displays 'Double!' if both dice show the same number. [5]
steps: Two separate dice, so two calls: die1 = random(1,6) and die2 = random(1,6) (1 mark each for correct range and storing).
Output: print the values using str() to join numbers to text (1 mark).
Selection: if die1 == die2 then print("Double!") (1 mark for correct comparison of the two stored values).

worked.ans:
chance = random(1,100)
if chance <= 20 then
   print("Bonus item!")
else
   print("Nothing this time")
endif
The range has 100 values and 20 of them (1 to 20) trigger the bonus, so the probability is 20/100 = 20%.
worked.q: A game gives the player a bonus item with a 20% chance each time they open a chest. Write code to decide whether the bonus is given. Explain why your range works. [4]
steps: 20% means 20 out of 100, so use random(1,100) (range of 100 equally likely values).
Condition: values 1 to 20 are 20 of the 100 values, so if chance <= 20 then give the bonus.
Alternative: random(1,5) == 1 also gives 1 in 5, which is 20%.

worked.ans: Error: the upper limit 8 is one too big (off-by-one error); random(0,8) can return 8, which is outside the array. Corrected: pick = random(0, 7) (or random(0, len(names) - 1)). Consequence: the program may crash with an index error when 8 is generated.
worked.q: A programmer wants to choose a random name from the array names, which holds 8 names indexed 0 to 7. They write: pick = random(0, 8) then print(names[pick]). Identify the error and write the corrected line. Explain what could happen. [3]
steps: Array has 8 items with indexes 0 to 7, so the highest index is 7.
random(0,8) is inclusive, so it can produce 8, an index that does not exist.
The program would then crash with an index out of range error (run-time error), but only some of the time, which makes it hard to spot.
Fix: use the length minus 1, or 7, as the upper limit.
